sections.description: Walks the reader through the patient’s background, exposure timeline, clinical features confirming anaphylaxis, and the first steps of resuscitation that reversed shock and hypoxemia. Sets the stage for later discussion of relapses.
subtopics: Pre-incident history relevant to risk and management (prior mild beta-lactam reaction, obesity, diabetes, medications)
Exposure timeline: clindamycin-associated rash; first-ever clarithromycin dose; symptom onset 1 hour post-ingestion
Clinical criteria establishing anaphylaxis (diffuse urticaria/erythema, hypotension, hypoxemia, facial swelling; no tongue/pharyngeal edema)
Immediate priorities and actions: IM epinephrine, high-flow oxygen, IV crystalloid bolus, H1 antihistamine; indicators of response
Rationale for admission to a monitored setting after initial stabilization

sections.section_title: Multiphasic Anaphylaxis—Definitions, Mechanisms, and Risk Stratification
sections.description: Defines biphasic and multiphasic anaphylaxis and distinguishes them from refractory or protracted reactions. Explains plausible mechanisms for relapses, timing, incidence, and risk factors, and applies these concepts to this case to justify monitoring intensity.
subtopics: Definitions and differentiation: biphasic and multiphasic relapse vs refractory or sustained anaphylaxis with ongoing absorption
Proposed mechanisms of relapse relevant to this case (late-phase mediator release; possible ongoing GI absorption of an oral drug; mast cell hyperreactivity)
Incidence and typical timing of recurrences; how the patient’s four episodes over ~12 hours fit known patterns
Suggested predictors of biphasic courses (severity, multiple epinephrine doses, delayed treatment) and which were present here
Observation strategy: rationale for prolonged monitored observation and escalation to ICU after the first relapse

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Workup and Reasoning: Tryptase, Culprit Identification, and Mast Cell Disease
sections.description: Details the ideal laboratory and consultative evaluation for complex anaphylaxis, how this case deviated, and how clinicians inferred the likely trigger. Explains why and how systemic mastocytosis was investigated and interpreted despite not meeting full criteria.
subtopics: Acute and convalescent tryptase testing: recommended timing (early sample, peak at 1–2 hours, baseline ≥24 hours post-resolution) and interpretation; deviations in this case and their implications
Reasoning supporting clarithromycin as the culprit (temporal relationship, no re-exposure, alternative explanations considered and deemed less likely)
Distinguishing true multiphasic relapse from sustained anaphylaxis due to ongoing oral drug absorption
When to evaluate for clonal mast cell disorders after severe/atypical anaphylaxis (elevated baseline tryptase, recurrent/severe episodes)

WHO systemic mastocytosis framework (major and minor criteria) and how this patient mapped (two minor criteria, major criterion not assessable; supportive findings such as hepatomegaly and persistently elevated tryptase)
Why confirmatory macrolide allergy testing was deferred; safe avoidance and documentation strategies

sections.section_title: Managing Relapses and Advanced Anaphylaxis Care
sections.description: Provides a structured approach to treating recurrent episodes, including correct epinephrine dosing, when to escalate to IV infusion, and the role of adjuncts and supportive care. Critically appraises the role of corticosteroids and integrates case-based decision-making.
subtopics: Repeat IM epinephrine: timing and dose; ensuring adult weight-appropriate dosing (0.01 mg/kg up to 0.5 mg) and access to 0.5 mg in adults >50 kg; implications of starting with 0.3 mg devices
Indications to escalate to IV epinephrine infusion (refractory hypotension after adequate IM dosing and fluids; recurrent severe episodes) and required monitoring
Adjuncts: roles and limitations of H1/H2 antihistamines for cutaneous symptoms and inhaled beta-agonists for bronchospasm
Corticosteroids: current evidence against routine use for preventing biphasic reactions; potential harms (e.g., hyperglycemia in diabetes); why steroids were nevertheless used here
Supportive care through relapses: oxygen titration, fluid resuscitation, airway readiness, frequent reassessment
Disposition decisions: indications for ICU admission; criteria to end observation (e.g., ≥24 hours symptom-free and hemodynamically stable)

sections.description: Summarizes the patient’s clinical course and discharge plan, outlines long-term management for suspected mast cell disease, and distills system-level lessons to improve future care of complex anaphylaxis.
subtopics: Clinical course resolution: decreasing severity of episodes, cessation of relapses, step-down after ~24 hours event-free, discharge on day 3

Discharge medications and equipment: levocetirizine initiation; epinephrine auto-injector prescription and training; consideration of dose selection based on body weight; recommendation to carry two devices
Follow-up pathway: allergy/immunology referral, serial baseline tryptase monitoring, consideration of repeat marrow evaluation/KIT testing if indicated, ongoing trigger avoidance (macrolides)
Patient education: early epinephrine use, EMS activation, written action plan, medical alert identification

System and team improvements: standardize tryptase sampling workflows, ensure availability/training for 0.5 mg adult epinephrine dosing, adopt risk-stratified observation protocols, contribute multiphasic cases to registries
